name: Resection Planning and Margins
title: Resection Planning and Margins
answer: Resection planning and margins covers the work of deciding, before and during an operation, how much tissue to remove and where the cut should run. In surgical robotics and navigation it joins preoperative imaging, tumour or lesion boundaries, and the anatomy that must be spared, so that a surgeon can see a planned volume rather than judge it by eye alone. The subject spans the planning software, the imaging it reads, the navigation hardware that tracks instruments in the room, and the pathology that later reports what the margin actually was. It matters most in cancer surgery, where leaving too little disease behind and taking too much healthy tissue carry different costs.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Resection planning and margins covers the work of deciding, before and during an operation, how much tissue to remove and where the cut should run. In surgical robotics and navigation it joins preoperative imaging, tumour or lesion boundaries, and the anatomy that must be spared, so that a surgeon can see a planned volume rather than judge it by eye alone. The subject spans the planning software, the imaging it reads, the navigation hardware that tracks instruments in the room, and the pathology that later reports what the margin actually was. It matters most in cancer surgery, where leaving too little disease behind and taking too much healthy tissue carry different costs.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The stack begins with cross sectional imaging such as CT or MRI, often fused with ultrasound or a prior scan, and with the segmentation that marks the target and the structures around it. Planning and navigation systems run on workstation class hardware in or near the operating theatre, sometimes with a cart mounted camera and tracked instruments for optical or electromagnetic localisation. Robotics platforms add arms and controllers, while the display links the planned volume to the patient's actual position through registration. Networks and image archives move studies between radiology, the planning station and the theatre, and latency and sterility constraints shape what can run where.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical path starts with segmentation of the lesion and adjacent critical structures, either by hand, by a learned model, or by a mix of both, followed by review and correction by a clinician. From that segmentation the team builds a target volume and a planned margin, then registers the plan to the patient using fiducials, surface matching or intraoperative imaging. Navigation then shows instrument position against the plan, and the surgeon may update the plan as tissue moves or as frozen section results arrive. Pathology later measures the true margin on the specimen, and that measurement is what closes the loop between the plan and the outcome.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The plan is a clinical document, so accountability sits with the treating clinician, not the software, and the segmentation and margin decisions need to be traceable to the images and settings that produced them. Devices used for planning or navigation generally fall under medical device regulation, which brings requirements for validation, labelling and change control, and the provenance of each scan, model version and edit matters when a case is reviewed. Patient data carries privacy and consent obligations, and shared or cloud based planning raises questions about where images rest and who can reach them. A margin reported by a model is an estimate, and the pathology report remains the reference point.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Work is moving toward tighter coupling of imaging, navigation and pathology, so that predicted margins can be compared against measured ones and the planning models improved from that feedback. Intraoperative imaging and rapid tissue assessment are being folded into the same workflow, and registration is becoming less dependent on manual steps. Learned segmentation is spreading from research into routine planning, which shifts attention to how these tools are checked and how their uncertainty is shown to a surgeon. The open questions are less about raw capability than about trust, documentation and who carries responsibility when a plan and a specimen disagree.
